title: Getting started: top-down BPMN business model
content:
# Getting started: top-down BPMN business model

*(Based on: Bruce Silver (2011), BPMN Method & Style, 2nd edition, pp. 53–67)*

This application supports you with the information available. The information must be developed and defined in close cooperation with representatives of the involved business experts.

## 1. Define the process scope

**Tools → BPMN → Define process scope**

**Purpose:** All participants gain a consistent understanding of the business process boundaries and conditions. The process scope is the business ‘map’ on which all subsequent modelling steps are based.

## 2. Define up to 10 top-level activities (subprocesses)

**Tools → BPMN → Define main activities**

For every top-level activity, define the possible **end states**.

**Purpose:** Defining the main activities from the process scope makes the essential work steps of the business process visible to everyone. It creates a clear structure and enables the remaining details to be defined efficiently and purposefully.

## 3. Create the top-level BPMN business process

Create the top-level BPMN process from the results of steps 1 and 2.

### 3.1 Adopt the start event from step 1

**Rule:** Place a start event on the left, typically a Message Start Event when the process is triggered externally, for example by a customer.

### 3.2 Arrange the end events from step 1

**Rule:** Place all end events from step 1 on the right, with one End Event for each final process state.

### 3.3 Derive subprocesses from top-level activities

**Rule:**

- Every top-level activity from step 2 becomes a subprocess in the top-level BPMN diagram.
- Keep the same order as the list from step 2.
- No tasks and no details – only subprocesses.

**Target picture:** Start Event → Subprocess A → Subprocess B → Subprocess C → End Event(s)

### 3.4 Connect elements with sequence flows

**Rule:** Connect all subprocesses, gateways, start events, and end events with sequence flows. Alternative paths leaving a gateway are led to subsequent activities without a merge gateway.

### 3.5 Model the logic between subprocesses with gateways

#### 3.5.a Parallel gateway (AND)

**Rule:**

- Use a Parallel Gateway (AND) when subprocesses are independent and can run in parallel.
- If a subsequent activity requires completion of two or more parallel activities, use a Parallel Gateway to join them.

#### 3.5.b Gateways for multiple end events of a top-level activity

**Starting point:** In step 2, you defined multiple end states for a top-level activity, for example ‘application approved’ and ‘application rejected’.

**Rule:** In most cases, check the result status using an XOR Gateway (data-based Exclusive Gateway). An OR Gateway is appropriate only if several end states can be true simultaneously and the paths are not strictly exclusive; this is uncommon in traditional business processes.

**Gateway naming after Silver:**

- **With two end states:** Gateway label `‘[end state]?’`; gate labels `yes` / `no`, for example `approved?` with `yes`/`no`.
- **With more than two end states:** Gate labels `[end state 1]`, `[end state 2]`, `[end state 3]`; use a general gateway label such as `‘<object> status?’`, for example `‘application status?’`.

## 4. Iteratively work out the details of a process path

For the selected process path, progressively specify the detailed business flow across every involved subprocess.

### Procedure

- Work through the process path from start to finish.
- For every subprocess, add a **None Start Event**, the business activities, decisions, and relevant events.
- The **end events of a subprocess** arise from the end states defined in step 2.
- Refine the business process logic until the flow is clear and complete.

### Practical experience from Ludger Schönfeld

A detailed level (subprocess) typically includes **at most 10–15 activities**. If it becomes more complex, modularise the flow again and model it as a **further subprocess**. This keeps the model understandable, maintainable, and methodologically sound.

## 5. Add collaboration for more business context

Add interactions between external business roles and the business process using **Message Flows**.

**Procedure:**

- Show external business roles as **collapsed pools**.
- Message flows show business communication between the process and external roles.
- Give every message flow a **business-meaningful label** that describes the message content.

**Benefit:** This adds valuable business context and makes the external interactions relevant to the process flow visible.

## Important

A business process uses **terms from the business domain’s perspective**. Technical terms, IT system names, and internal system logic do **not** belong in the business flow.

**Goal:** Ensure the readability and comprehensibility of the business process logic for all participants, regardless of technical knowledge.

## Further reading: apply BPMN & DMN sustainably

If you want not only to model BPMN and DMN but also to implement them sustainably in business process applications, the German-language book **Business Process Automation** presents a complete, pragmatic approach. It explains how to elicit business processes systematically, define them correctly with BPMN, and then implement them flexibly, transparently, efficiently, and maintainably using **process-driven architecture**, based on Dr. Volker Stiehl’s process-driven approach.

[Business Process Automation – sustainable business-process automation with BPMN and DMN at Rheinwerk Verlag](https://www.rheinwerk-verlag.de/5716)

title: Model BPMN processes
content:
# Model BPMN processes

Create process steps with the palette on the left and connect them using sequence flows.

- Select an element to edit it.
- The right-click context menu lets you **colour**, **copy**, **cut**, and **paste** selected elements.
- A colour action applies to every selected BPMN element. Choose **Default** to remove the colour marking.
- Copied BPMN elements remain in the BPMN clipboard and cannot be pasted into a DMN model.
- Use **Tools → BPMN → Define process scope** or **Define main activities** to record business information.
- The main-activities dialog supports at most ten activities. For every activity, enter its name, short description, end events, and the next activity or final end event. **Apply** stores the localized Markdown map and saves the BPMN file.

## Subprocesses

When you open a subprocess, a navigation path appears at the top of the modelling area. Select the parent-process name to return to it.

The **token simulator** optionally visualises a flow and does not change the model contents.

## Token simulator

Activate it through **Tools → BPMN → Enable token simulator**; simulation mode opens immediately. The menu item then changes to **Disable token simulator**. A process with a **None Start Event** starts automatically. For a **Message Start Event**, trigger the visible Play icon at the start event; the message is intentionally not created automatically. For its normal flow, an embedded subprocess needs a None Start Event with an outgoing sequence flow. A Call Activity is simulated as a single activity; a linked BPMN model is not loaded into the simulation.

title: Paragraphs in main activities
content:
# Paragraphs in main activities

Under **Tools → BPMN → Define main activities**, a short description can contain multiple paragraphs. All paragraphs remain after **Apply**, saving, closing, and reopening.
